# Introduction
\vspace{-6mm}

For Aim 1, we will be testing the hypothesis that memory consolidation and AD-signature corticol thickness can be predicted by higher baseline cytokine and chemokine levels.
We will additionally assess whether decreases in episodic memory and corticol thickness over a one year period are associated with increases in cytokine and chemokine levels.

## Data Analysis
\vspace{-6mm}


For these analyses, we will use a longitudinal linear mixed effects model for each outcome of interest. 
The primary outcomes of interest are IL-6, TNF-$\alpha$, MCD-1, and Eotaxin-1. 
The primary explanatory variables (PEVs) of interest consist of the 9 memory consolidation variables and the measure of gray matter corticol thickness. 
We will adjust for age and sex in these models. 
Additional variables that are available include education, BMI, blood presure, history of hypercholesterolemia, APOE genotype,
Clinical Dementia Rating, Geriartric Depression Scale, the use of Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory drugs,
cognitive measurements including MoCA and a neurophysioogical assessment, 
information on recent infections and illnesses, surgical procedures in the past year, autoimmune conditions, 
and lastly, diagnostic information.
The number of all possible covariates sums to approximately 25. 
As this is a large number of variables, we will first focus on the 9 memory consolidation variables and determine if the number can be reduced. For this, we will create a correlation matrix of all 9 variables. 
We will then assess if a reduction of these variables results in a more simple and homogeneous (COME BACK FOROGOT THIS WORD) model by conducting Partial F-Tests to identify if the addition of consolidation variables are meaningful. 
After we reduce the PEVs, we will repeat the same process for the 14 additional variables. 
These tests will allow us to identify the most parsimonious and simple model for
the research questions of interest.

## Power Analysis

We note that although, the planned primary analysis uses a longitudinal model to estimate mean change from baseline to 1 year, we will use a baseline-adjusted multiple linear regression model for power analyses. 
This model closely mirrors the longitudinal change analysis as there are only two time points that are observed.
